title: The Rakab Ganj wall
hook: the demolition of a gurdwara wall in Delhi stirred protest

segments.voice: Yesterday, presses and papers, and your line was print spreads it. Did you read one Punjabi word in its own letters? Today, news that the papers carried quickly, about a wall in Delhi. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

Workmen arrive at a gurdwara in Delhi with orders and tools. A new capital is being laid out nearby, with grand avenues and government buildings, and the gurdwara's outer wall is in the way of the plan. The wall comes down. On paper, it's a small thing: some bricks, a boundary, a straighter line on a map. But the place inside that wall is where, Sikhs remember, a Guru's body was cremated in secret, at great risk, by people who loved him. Today: the Rakab Ganj wall.
screen: `WORKMEN WITH ORDERS.` → `A WALL IN THE WAY OF A PLAN.` → `WHAT THE WALL ENCLOSED.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where, tradition says, the body of Guru Tegh Bahadur was cremated after his execution in Delhi. Sikhs remember him as the Guru who gave his life rather than see others forced from their faith. Tradition remembers a trader with a train of ox-carts, Lakhi Shah Vanjara, carrying the body away under cover of a storm and setting fire to his own house so the Guru could be cremated without the authorities knowing. A house burned to honor a Guru. That's what the ground means. Second, the wall. When the British laid out the new capital, an outer wall of the gurdwara was knocked down to fit the plan. To the planners it was a boundary. To Sikhs it was the edge of holy ground, and taking it down without care felt like contempt for the Guru's memory. Third, the protest. Sikhs wrote, petitioned and met, and the papers you heard about yesterday spread the news. Some argued for caution and patience. Others insisted that a Sikh holy place couldn't be treated this way and that the community had to stand up. The wall became a test of whether Sikhs could protect their own sacred places. In the end, the wall was rebuilt. Fourth, why a wall matters. The Gurus taught that the Divine is everywhere, not trapped in bricks. Yet Sikhs honor places where the Gurus lived and gave their lives, because memory needs somewhere to stand. A wall says: here, something happened that we won't let anyone forget. The wall mattered, and the protest over it pointed toward bigger struggles to come.
screen: `WHERE A GURU WAS CREMATED.` · `A BOUNDARY, KNOCKED DOWN.` · `PETITIONS, PAPERS, PROTEST.` · `MEMORY NEEDS SOMEWHERE TO STAND.` · then, large: `THE WALL MATTERED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a small sacred thing. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one small thing that's sacred to you or to someone you love: a prayer book, a photograph, a grave, a corner of a room, a ring, a gutka with worn pages. Picture it clearly. Notice how easily it could be moved, thrown out, or treated carelessly by someone who doesn't know what it means. Breathe slowly with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. After the bell, do one thing to protect it. The bell holds the time.
The Rakab Ganj wall. The outer wall of the Delhi gurdwara where, tradition says, Guru Tegh Bahadur was cremated; knocked down for a city plan, protested, and rebuilt. Today's word.
Your line: the wall mattered. Today, protect one small sacred thing: put it somewhere safe, clean it, or tell someone what it means. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib in New Delhi is visited by Sikhs and others who come to remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, listen to kirtan and eat in the langar; it is remembered alongside Gurdwara Sis Ganj, where the Guru was executed.
